source_text: Verum sufficiant ista de muliere, transeamus ad viri munia. Adae - inquit - dixit: Maledicta terra in operibus tuis; in tristitia manducabis eam omnibus diebus vitae tuae; spinas et tribulos edet tibi, et edes fenum agri tui; in sudore faciei tuae edes panem tuum, donec convertaris in terram de qua sumptus es; quoniam terra es, et in terram ibis [n168] . Hic non est dictum: Multiplicabo spinas tuas, aut sudores tuos; sed quasi tunc primum creata dicuntur. At etiam huius invidia, non maiore quam uxoris eius labore dissolvitur; initio quippe non semini hominis, sed humo maledicitur: In tuis operibus -inquit - maledicta terra erit. Quid commerita fuerant arva (quae certe de traduce Adae habere nihil poterant), ut pro peccato voluntatis alienae convicium maledictionis exciperent? An ut etiam ipsorum cespitum doceretur exemplo, posse esse maledictum, ubi culpa non esset? Nam si in homine peccatum, in segete maledictum, manifestum est crimina non semper adhaerere dispendiis. Si ergo propter hoc maledicitur terrae, ut ille qui peccaverat affligatur, nec tamen ibi iniquitas, ubi maledictio continetur; cur non ea conditione, etiamsi quid aerumnarum naturae nostrae post peccatum primi hominis doceretur illatum, tamen sequeretur non ideo miseros esse nascentes, ut rei convincerentur; sed ut commemoratione peccati primi, afflictio succedanea his quos reos non fecerat, imitationis malae indiceret cautionem? Quandoquidem et terra ob hoc ostenderetur maledicti convicium pertulisse, ut malum alienae voluntatis argueret, non ut participationem sui criminis gigneret; nisi forte credamus cariorem Deo terram esse, quam innocentiam, ut scelere alieno cum glebam non patiatur pollui, addici tamen permittat infantiam. Maledictum ergo dirigitur in terram, nec tamen hoc ipsum relinquitur involutum. Disseritur quippe quo fine eiusmodi sententia tenderetur, vel quomodo humus maledicta vocaretur. In tristitia - inquit - manducabis eam omnibus diebus vitae tuae. Quo igitur genere se exponat, advertito; maledicta dicitur terra, non quo in eam animadverti quiverit, sed hoc nomine opinio animi maerentis ostenditur; ut quoniam sterilem sciebat pro cultoris sui meritis, aegritudo esurientis operarii imputaret terrae quod ipse promeruerat, et maledictam eam afflictus vocaret, cuius ideo claudebatur opimitas, ut praevaricator ille nec naturam, nec terram, sed voluntatem atque personam suam maledicto fateretur obnoxiam. Spinas - inquit - et tribulos edet tibi. Non fuit contentus dicere: Spinas et tribulos edet; sed addidit: tibi. Inter virgulta quippe alia, et veprium frutices olim iussa protulerat; tunc vero, ut compungeretur homo, solito senticosior futura promittitur. Quod Adam vehementer castigare poterat, quem post paradisi fontes et prata, etiam unus rubus posset offendere. In sudore autem faciei tuae edes panem tuum; non satis ad aerumnam video pertinere; siquidem etiam naturale adiumentum est, ut operantium artus sudore recreentur. Illi autem ante peccatum laborem incubuisse culturae lectio ipsa testatur. Sic enim ait: Et sumpsit Dominus Deus hominem quem fecit, et posuit illum in paradiso, operari eum et custodire [n169] . Si ergo etiam in paradiso noluit eum Deus pabula examussim illaborata suscipere, sed indicto operationis, quam indiderat excitavit industriam; quid ei novum accidisse credimus, si sentiret sudorem, qui experiebatur laborem? Sequitur autem: Donec convertaris in terram ex qua sumptus es; quoniam terra es, et in terram ibis. Haec sane pars extrema sententiae, sicut illa mulieris, ad indicium, non ad supplicium respicit; quin immo, ut res indicat, promisso fine consolatur hominem. Quia enim supra commemoraverat dolores, labores, sudores, quorum sensum natura, nimietatem persona susceperat; ne hoc in aeternum videretur extendi, mitificat aegritudinem terminus indicatus; ac si diceret: Verum non semper ista patieris; sed donec convertaris in terram de qua sumptus es; quia terra es - inquit - et in terram ibis. Cur non, postquam dixit: donec convertaris in terram de qua sumptus es, subdidit: Quia peccasti et mea praecepta transgressus es? Hoc enim dicendum erat, si resolutio corporum ad crimina pertineret. Verum quid dixit? Quia terra es - inquit - et in terram ibis. Causam cur in terram rediturus esset, ostendit: Quia terra es, inquit. Quomodo autem esset terra, superior sermo patefecerat: Quia de terra - inquit - sumptus es. Si ergo redeundi in terram, hanc esse rationem dixit Deus, quoniam fuerat assumptus e terra, porro ut assumeretur, ad iniquitatem spectare non potuit; procul dubio non iniquitatis, sed naturae mortalis fuit, ut qui aeternus non erat, in corporis parte solveretur. Illa ergo sterilitas arborum, illa veprium ubertas, illa aegri partus aucta calamitas, personis hominum sunt illata, non generi. Denique iam natis Cain et Abel unius naturae ambobus, sed diversarum voluntatum, nec Cain sponte peccanti profuit quod eum peccata patris non presserant, nec Abeli nocuit quod parentes eius deliquerant; sed suopte uterque iudicio nec virtutis sibi, nec vitii naturale infuisse praeiudicium vario proposito, fine vario publicarunt. Functi quippe officio sacerdotum, conditori suo Deo hostias obtulerunt. Ceterum par obsequium, impar cura discrevit. Patefecit hoc divina sententia, quae complacitum sibi munus Abelis ostendit; offenso autem Cain causam suae indignationis aperuit, dicens eum bene obtulisse, sed male divisisse. Nec mora exarsit profanus animus in livorem, et germani sanctitate gravatus, parricidium gratificatur invidiae. Ita prima occasione claruit malum non esse mortem, quod eam iustus primus omnium dedicavit. Nec tamen iram Dei animi sontis audacia effugit. Interrogatur de fratre, convincitur de scelere, addicitur ultioni, et extra eum terrorem, qui ei pro insigni crudelitatis incubuit, terrae quoque maledictione punitur: Maledictus - inquit - tu a terra, quae aperuit os suum accipere sanguinem fratris tui de tua manu; quoniam operaberis terram, et non adiciet virtutem suam dare tibi [n170] . Ecce denuo sterilitas terrae in poena cultoris indicitur. Innumera autem generis tormenta in Deuteronomio promittuntur. Quid ergo? Nostrarum dumeta terrarum, quibus amputandis runcone armatus cultor invigilat, per Cain parricidium germinarunt? Et quia omnis spinosi ruris dominus, peccato quod spinarum ubertate punitum est, a vobis putatur obnoxius; omnes iam parvuli non solum comedisse poma, quamvis nascantur sine dentibus, sed etiam Abelis sanguinem effudisse dicentur? Apparet certe, ad quem furorem perveniat Manichaeorum tradux; quae quoniam nihil habet praeter amentiam, ridet de argumentis vestris Catholicorum gravitas; sed de ruinis vestris eorumdem plorat affectio.
pass_a_gloss: But let those things suffice about the woman, let us pass to the offices of the man. To Adam, it says, he said: Cursed is the earth in your works; in sadness you will eat it all the days of your life; it will eat out thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the hay of your field; in the sweat of your face you will eat your bread, until you are turned into the earth from which you were taken; because you are earth, and into earth you will go. Here it was not said: I will multiply your thorns, or your sweats; but they are said as then first created. But even the spite of this is dissolved by no greater labor than of his wife; for in the beginning it is cursed not to the seed of the human, but to the soil: In your works, it says, the earth will be cursed. What had the fields deserved (which certainly could have nothing from Adam's tradux), that they would receive the insult of a curse for the sin of another's will? Or that even by the example of those turfs themselves it would be taught that there can be a curse where there would not be a fault? For if in the human sin, in the crop a curse, it is manifest that charges do not always cling to losses. If therefore on account of this the earth is cursed, that he who had sinned may be afflicted, nor nevertheless is iniquity there where a curse is contained; why not by that condition, even if something of hardships were taught inflicted on our nature after the first human's sin, nevertheless it would follow that those being born are not therefore miserable, that they would be convicted guilty; but that by a commemoration of the first sin a succeeding affliction would declare a caution of an evil imitation to those whom it had not made guilty? Since indeed even the earth would be shown to have borne the insult of a curse on account of this, that it would accuse the evil of another's will, not that it would generate a participation of its own charge; unless perhaps we believe the earth is dearer to God than innocence, so that he does not suffer a clod to be polluted with another's crime, yet permits infancy to be assigned. A curse therefore is directed into the earth, nor nevertheless is this itself left involved. For it is discussed to what end a sentence of this kind would be stretched, or how the soil would be called cursed. In sadness, he says, you will eat it all the days of your life. By which kind therefore it explains itself, attend; the earth is said cursed, not by which it could be noticed into it, but by this name the opinion of a mourning mind is shown; so that because he knew it sterile for the deserts of its cultivator, the sickness of a hungry worker would impute to the earth what he himself had deserved, and afflicted would call it cursed, whose richness was therefore being closed, that that prevaricator would confess not nature, nor the earth, but his will and person liable to a curse. Thorns, he says, and thistles it will eat out for you. He was not content to say: It will eat out thorns and thistles; but he added: for you. For among other shrubs, and the bushes of brambles it had of old been commanded to bring forth; but then, that the human might be pricked, it is promised about to be more thorny than usual. Which could vehemently chastise Adam, whom after the fountains and meadows of paradise even one bramble could offend. But in the sweat of your face you will eat your bread; I do not see it pertains enough to hardship; since indeed it is even a natural help, that the limbs of those working are recreated by sweat. But that labor of culture hung over him before sin the reading itself testifies. For thus it says: And the Lord God took the human whom he made, and placed him in paradise, to work it and to keep it. If therefore even in paradise God was unwilling that he receive foods exactly unlabored, but by an indicated operation he stirred the industry which he had put in; what do we believe happened new to him, if he would feel sweat, who was experiencing labor? But it follows: Until you are turned into the earth from which you were taken; because you are earth, and into earth you will go. This last part of the sentence indeed, as that of the woman, looks to an indication, not to a punishment; nay rather, as the matter indicates, it consoles the human by a promised end. Because he had commemorated above pains, labors, sweats, whose sense nature, whose excess a person had taken up; lest this seem to be extended into eternity, an indicated limit mildens the sickness; as if he were saying: But you will not always suffer these things; but until you are turned into the earth from which you were taken; because you are earth, he says, and into earth you will go. Why did he not, after he said: until you are turned into the earth from which you were taken, subjoin: Because you sinned and transgressed my precepts? For this ought to have been said, if the resolution of bodies pertained to charges. But what did he say? Because you are earth, he says, and into earth you will go. He showed the cause why he would be about to return into earth: Because you are earth, he says. But how he would be earth, the earlier speech had laid open: Because from earth, he says, you were taken. If therefore God said this is the reason of returning into earth, because he had been taken up from earth, further that he would be taken up could not look to iniquity; without doubt it was not of iniquity, but of a mortal nature, that he who was not eternal would be loosed in the part of the body. That sterility therefore of trees, that richness of brambles, that increased calamity of a sick birth, were inflicted on the persons of humans, not on the genus. Finally already Cain and Abel having been born, both of one nature, but of diverse wills, neither did it profit Cain sinning spontaneously that his father's sins had not pressed him, nor did it harm Abel that his parents had offended; but each by his own judgment published by a various purpose, a various end, that a natural prior judgment neither of virtue nor of vice had been in him. For having performed the office of priests, they offered victims to God their founder. For the rest an equal obedience, an unequal care distinguished. The divine sentence laid this open, which showed Abel's gift pleasing to itself; but to offended Cain it opened the cause of its indignation, saying he had offered well, but had divided evilly. Nor delay, a profane mind burned into envy, and weighed by a brother's holiness, he gratifies parricide to spite. Thus by the first occasion it became clear that death is not evil, because the just first of all dedicated it. Nor nevertheless did the daring of a guilty mind flee God's wrath. He is asked about his brother, he is convicted of a crime, he is assigned to vengeance, and besides that terror which hung over him for a mark of cruelty, he is punished also by a curse of the earth: Cursed, he says, are you from the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand; because you will work the earth, and it will not add its virtue to give to you. Behold again a sterility of the earth is declared in the penalty of the cultivator. But countless torments of the genus are promised in Deuteronomy. What therefore? Did the thickets of our lands, for cutting which a cultivator armed with a bill-hook watches, germinate through Cain's parricide? And because every lord of a thorny countryside is thought by you liable to the sin which was punished by a richness of thorns; will all little ones already be said not only to have eaten fruits, although they are born without teeth, but even to have poured out Abel's blood? It certainly appears to what fury the tradux of the Manichaeans arrives; which since it has nothing besides madness, the gravity of the Catholics laughs at your arguments; but the affection of the same weeps at your ruins.

pass_b_english: Enough about the woman; let us pass to the man’s tasks. ‘To Adam he said: The earth is cursed in your works. In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of your field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth, and into earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3:17–19). Here he did not say, ‘I will multiply your thorns or your sweat’; they are spoken of as though first created then. Yet this objection is removed with no greater effort than in his wife’s case.

First, it is not the human’s seed but the soil that is cursed: ‘The earth will be cursed in your works.’ What had the fields done to deserve the insult of a curse for the sin of someone else’s will, when they certainly could inherit nothing from Adam? Was it to teach by the very sods that a curse can exist where no fault exists? If sin was in the human but the curse in the crop, plainly guilt does not always attach to loss.

If the earth is cursed to afflict the sinner, while iniquity is not located where the curse is, why could the same condition not apply even if some miseries were shown to have been imposed on our nature after the first human’s sin? It would not follow that newborns are miserable to prove them guilty. Rather, by recalling the first sin, suffering handed down could warn against evil imitation those whom it had not made guilty. The earth likewise would be shown to have endured the insult of a curse to condemn the evil of another’s will, not to generate participation in its own guilt. Unless perhaps we believe soil dearer to God than innocence, so that while he does not allow another’s crime to pollute a clod, he nevertheless permits it to condemn infancy!

The curse is directed at the earth, then, but even this is not left unexplained. The purpose of the pronouncement and the way the soil is called cursed are set out: ‘In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life.’ Notice how he explains himself. The earth is called cursed not because punishment could be inflicted on it, but because this name expresses the opinion of a grieving mind. Knowing it barren because of its cultivator’s deserts, the hungry worker in his distress would blame the soil for what he had himself deserved. Afflicted, he would call it cursed. Its fertility was withheld precisely so that the transgressor should acknowledge neither nature nor earth, but his own will and person, as subject to the curse.

‘It shall produce thorns and thistles for you.’ He was not content to say, ‘It shall produce thorns and thistles,’ but added ‘for you.’ Long before, at the command, the earth had produced thorny bushes among its other plants. Now, to sting the human being, it was promised to be thornier than usual. This could chastise Adam severely: after paradise’s springs and meadows, even one bramble could offend him.

But ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread’ does not seem to me especially connected with misery. Sweat is even a natural aid, refreshing the limbs of workers. The text itself testifies that cultivation’s labor lay upon him before sin: ‘The Lord God took the human he had made and placed him in paradise to work and guard it’ (Genesis 2:15). Even in paradise, then, God did not want him to receive food with absolutely no labor, but by requiring work stirred the industry he had implanted. What new thing do we believe happened if someone who experienced labor also felt sweat?

It continues: ‘Until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ This last part of the pronouncement, like the woman’s, concerns information, not punishment. Indeed, as the matter shows, it comforts the human by promising an end. Above, it had recalled pains, labors, and sweat, whose sensation nature received and whose excess the person received. Lest these seem to extend forever, the announced limit softens the distress—as though to say: You will not always suffer these things, but only until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth and into earth you shall go.

After saying, ‘Until you return to the earth from which you were taken,’ why did he not add, ‘Because you sinned and transgressed my commands’? That should have been said if bodily dissolution belonged to crimes. What did he say instead? ‘Because you are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ He showed the reason for returning to earth: ‘Because you are earth.’ The earlier words explained how he was earth: ‘Because you were taken from earth.’ If God said the reason for returning to earth was having been taken from earth, and that taking could not concern iniquity, then beyond doubt bodily dissolution in one who was not eternal belonged to mortal nature, not iniquity.

That barrenness of trees, abundance of thorns, and increased distress of painful childbirth were therefore imposed on particular people, not the race. When Cain and Abel were born, both shared one nature but had different wills. Cain, sinning voluntarily, gained nothing from the fact that his father’s sins did not burden him; Abel suffered no harm from his parents’ wrongdoing. Each, by personal judgment, through a different purpose and outcome, publicly showed that neither virtue nor vice carried a natural determination within him.

Performing priests’ work, they offered sacrifices to God their creator. Unequal care distinguished their outwardly equal service. God’s pronouncement made this clear, showing Abel’s gift pleased him. To the offended Cain he explained his displeasure: Cain had offered rightly but divided wrongly. Immediately the impious mind blazed with envy and, burdened by his brother’s holiness, gratified envy with a brother’s murder. Thus at the first occasion it became clear that death is not evil, since a righteous person was the first of all to undergo it.

Yet the guilty mind’s audacity did not escape God’s anger. Cain was questioned about his brother, convicted of his crime, and sentenced to punishment. Besides the terror laid upon him as the mark of his cruelty, he was punished by a curse from the earth: ‘You are cursed from the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work the earth, it shall no longer give you its strength’ (Genesis 4:3–12). See, once again the earth’s barrenness is decreed as the cultivator’s punishment. Countless kinds of torments are also threatened in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 28:15–68).

What then? Did the thickets in our fields, which the farmer labors to cut back with his billhook, sprout through Cain’s murder? Since you think every owner of thorny land liable for the sin punished by abundant thorns, will all infants now be said not only to have eaten fruit, though born toothless, but also to have shed Abel’s blood? The madness reached by Manichaean inherited sin is clear. Since it contains nothing but insanity, catholics’ sober judgment laughs at your arguments; yet those same people’s affection weeps over your ruin.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
